text: Thank you, everyone, for coming to this talk and Devanj for organizing this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Raghav.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm a staff machine learning engineer at DoorDash.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I work on search and personalization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Today I'm gonna talk about the ways that we're integrating LLMs for our marketplace discovery, specifically in four pieces, and how these primitives are kind of working towards our integration of LLMs into traditional RECs as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I'll start off today with a simple claim.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The claim is that to build effective discovery,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In this case, for a marketplace like DoorDash, the real bottleneck is semantic understanding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, that is knowing what, you know, actually, what items mean for users, given some context, and what a shopper actually intends to do on an app like DoorDash.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And historically, we have treated these as engagement optimization problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: However, LLMs give us a genuinely new lever to extend this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this talk is about the four primitives that have allowed us to start leveraging LLMs for problems at DoorDash.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As you may know, DoorDash is now grown well beyond restaurants.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're in grocery, retail, pets, gifting, and more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And our goal is to capture every shoppable moment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we know that across these verticals, the users frequently have very broad shopping missions, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, a consumer may say when they come to our app is, you know, I just adopted a puppy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What do I need to get started this week?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this consumer may start on searching for puppy food because they just adopted the puppy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That one query could unfold into further query reformulations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They land on collections for other shopping needs, complementary items such as crates, leashes, training pads, all the way to checkout.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this could happen over multiple sessions, multiple days, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And capturing that whole arc is pretty hard because it spans multiple models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where the four primitives I will cover come in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Specifically supervision, catalog semantics, semantic personalization, and steerable content generation, as we heard previously as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a system of shared representations that help us map this customer's journey with the use of LLMs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, with supervision, the question we're asking or looking to address is how do we teach our retrieval and ranking systems what good means for different tasks?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And here's a simple example, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A shopper searches for gluten-free pasta, and if we only rank from engagement, very popular regular spaghettis might show up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because it sells well, you know, it may continue to show up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even gluten-free white bread might be retrieved and show up because it overlaps with gluten-free.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But neither of these are clearly the right answer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What we actually want is graded relevance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A true gluten-free pasta should be a high relevance item.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Chickpea pasta might be a reasonable substitute.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And regular spaghetti, while it's popular, it fails the constraint that the user has.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, to solve this, there are obviously two sources of truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We could look at human annotation, but that's expensive, slow, and becomes quickly stale because our catalog changes quite rapidly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second is behavioral signals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're abundant, but obviously, as I mentioned, biased by exposure, position, price, promotions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: and previous model choices.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the missing signal is a scalable reasoning signal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where LLMs are very useful as they offer a way to produce that supervision for such tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in our case, the pipeline starts with human ground truths.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We build a high-quality seed set of example query item pairs on a three-level relevant scale, 0, 1, 2.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We audit the suspicious cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, if a human label says that an item is irrelevant, but that item performs very well on add to cart or conversions, we send that case to a stronger LLM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To reevaluate with more granular prompts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also reconcile with other models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, our query to taxonomy or category models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if a query maps to a set of valid categories and the items belong to those valid categories, we may adjust the label accordingly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And through this process, we're able to achieve a pretty high precision golden data set.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That we then fine-tune a lightweight LLM, let's say, for example, a GPT-4.0 mini, on top of it, and that's when it really pays off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are able to use that fine-tuned labeler offline across our full catalog to generate full graded query item pairs, and those labels become one shared target for both retrieval and ranking systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This pattern has been pretty important for us over the past few years.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Use expensive reasoning once offline, then distill it into models that can be served cheaply and quickly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now let's take retrieval first.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The challenge is standard embeddings at e-commerce scale quickly collapse the relevance distinction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Items that are merely related sit close to items that actually match, and the model may know two items are related but not be able to separate exact matches, substitutes, complements.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So our fix is a two-stage contrastive method trained on the same graded labels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Stage one, which we call mining, does a global geometry shaping.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We use two tower encoders with multi-level supervised contrastive loss.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: After that we use that base model to mine harder negatives and these are items that the model confuses.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Hard negatives that are ranked too high or strong positives ranked too low.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the second stage after that is where we really put the model through curriculum training, use those hard negatives, relabel them, and our relevance of our retrieval layer improves sharply after that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So after stage one, we see overlaps between relevant and moderately relevant, but after stage two, there is a significant difference.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this has been one of our biggest levers
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Retrieval improvement across the board.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've improved NDCG of relevance by 2.3%, and that's also been true with our downstream business metrics.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we did the same exercise with our ranking models as well, distilling LLM reasoned labels into our rankers, however, combining this with business and engagement objectives.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here we add a new tower, in this case an ordinal relevance tower on top of the LLM graded labels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this prediction sits right alongside existing engagement towers, click, add to cart, and conversion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And since they share the same bottom layers, the semantic fit and relevance fit gets distilled in the same backward pass, and our model is able to predict probability of relevance across the different levels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we are able to blend through a value function on top of this that allows us to fine-tune between engagement and relevance for different surfaces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, these two examples are part of a larger theme of our work across similar projects.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Where it seems right, we're not replacing the retrieval and ranking system with an LLM, but rather distilling the reasoning and understanding into some production ranking architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this allows us to kind of quickly test and also scalably improve our models with LLMs while keeping the business and system objectives of these surfaces in mind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So once we have supervision, the next question is, how do we represent a very large and constantly changing catalog in a way that every model, be it language models or traditional retrieval and ranking models, that they can understand?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And at DoorDash's scale, you can imagine we're kind of surfacing items across stores, internationally, actually, now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's easily a few billion items at the store item level.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for these items, you obviously have unique SKU IDs, but it says nothing semantically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we also have a human-curated taxonomy that helps us classify and categorize these items into meaningful spaces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But often this is too coarse and too rigid.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example, something like hot sauces may just have like sauces, hot sauces in the taxonomy, but it doesn't tell you anything about the relationship between Hoifeng or Franks or Tabasco.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's where we've also adapted or adopted semantic IDs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's been introduced previously already.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a backbone for a lot of our work now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What it does is it gives us a short hierarchical code that's analogous to our taxonomy but the ability to control the fine-grained nature of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the result of this learned taxonomy is that each item gets this hierarchical code and the prefix captures broad neighborhoods and the later tokens capture finer distinctions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for example in the map over on the slide you'll see hot sauces and the structure emerging from the data with zero labels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Each one share the same first and second prefix in this ID sequence but then split by speciality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now you've got Mexican, Caribbean, Korean hot sauces being split up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the important property is that this code that's learned is comparable, as I said, by prefix, but also usable by all of our downstream models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that unlocks a few things for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first is cross-category comparisons or relationships.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You know, chips, salsa, guacamole may live in different taxonomy branches, but a shared semantic ID neighborhood can indicate that they belong together in maybe a shopping mission.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, cold start problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Oftentimes, we get new catalog items added by stores.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with techniques like ngram and byte parent coding, of these tokens, we're able to scalably add these to our models as sparse ID features.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, tail coverage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So sparse items inherit a lot of signal from semantically related items.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we don't have to wait for the volume or exposure to consumers for these items.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly, nice to have is the fact that we can actually also do a reverse audit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we can audit our catalog and how well our human labels agree with these semantically learned labels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a couple of examples of where we're using it today, just to give some real metrics.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has been one of our biggest improvements to our rancor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In this case, it's actually improved our rancor by improving MRR between 4% to 5%, and that's translated to pretty big conversion wins as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second one that I'm particularly fond of is query reformulation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, again, going back to the hot sauce example, Sriracha can lead to chili garlic sauce or sambal olek.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And because these queries map onto our catalog-grounded semantic neighborhood, that results in much more relevant queries that we're suggesting to users.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Ultimately, if these are queries that we don't have inventory for on DoorDash, they're meaningless.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with the addition of semantic IDs in this query graph, we were actually able to see pretty massive MRR gains as well for this piece of work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for now, we've talked about item mapping and relevance, and the next question is consumer context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What does the system know?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: about the shopper, and can that knowledge be reused across models again?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where our third primitive comes in, memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So memory in the agentic context is pretty well understood now.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We apply the same concepts to our recommendation systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So user embeddings are clearly very useful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have many representations of our consumers, but they don't necessarily get to why a consumer may have certain intents and why they might have certain preferences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Additionally, LLMs cannot readily use these embeddings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You could tokenize and train these models to learn it, but oftentimes, having some explicit LLM-native counterpart is very useful, and that's what we have found.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the idea of memory is to represent the consumer in multiple forms, semantic, inspectable, and reusable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the way we think about memory is in three timescales.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So long-term memory captures durable preferences from orders, searches, browsing, support interactions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Real-time context captures agentic interactions, sorry, in-session interactions, so cart state, active searches.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we have stated preferences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: which come from agentic interactions, so something like AskDoordash, for example, where consumers are able to explicitly state their constraints and preferences as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the way we represent consumers in this long-term memory is through memory blocks, and these are structured in a way that allows us to add new dimensions of the user from dietary preferences to dining preferences to substitute preferences as we learn more about the consumer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that is decoupled from the downstream system that doesn't need to reinterpret this for their own use cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So each consumer's memory is materialized in multiple forms.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So first is text.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's human readable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It captures the consumer in a compact way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second are latent vectors, embeddings of those memory blocks that can be fed into retrieval and ranking systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third are graph and tree or hierarchical approaches.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So type relationships between consumers and brands, taxonomies, and memory revealed preferences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these are assembled into composite memory objects that both ML models and LLMs use downstream.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So an example is this context graph where we connect consumers with extracted memory concepts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a graph fits neatly into shopping journeys because oftentimes consumer item interactions are sparse and multi-hop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in this case, these context graphs are able to link consumers across memory concepts that we previously did not have relationships for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's particularly helpful at fine-grained taxonomy levels.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In our case, we're seeing for retrieval using graph-based embeddings outperforming our existing taxonomy-based embeddings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today, this memory framework shows up in three places.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first is personalized collections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll talk about that a bit later.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second is agentic personalization, so AskDoordash, for example, uses this to personalize its sessions for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third, in retrieval and ranking models, as I said, we encode these memory blocks and feed them as features in downstream models as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the fourth primitive is steerable content generation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We heard quite a bit about it in the previous talk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this slide is my take on how we're piecing all these primitives together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So...
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of these inputs, semantic IDs, memory blocks, and graded relevance or LLM supervision feed into multiple models, be it LLMs or small language models or traditional models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And from these inputs we can generate different output shapes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Ranked semantic ID lists, carousel titles, sub copies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these show up across different surfaces today on DoorDash.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A direct example of this is our personalized collections on store pages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Historically, collections on store pages on DoorDash have been a fixed library or attribute-based, and we've been able to expand that through consumer-level collection generation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today this is an offline LLM process where we take in consumer memory, semantic IDs, and synthesize collections all the way from title, subtitle, to the actual items.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the important part is that control and steerability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're able to react to occasions and moments and build those collections as needed for different consumers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At serving time, because this is all batch and generated offline through LLMs, we are able to still use our existing retrieval and ranking stack for item hydration, collection ranking, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is, for example, what a shopper actually sees.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For a shopper with plant-based affinity, the system can generate plant-based pantry rows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For cat-only households, it can generate cat-drive food rows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if a session indicates that a person is going through pantry restocking, it can bias towards pantry staples.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And our early tests show that consumers are feeling the benefits of these tailored experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An example is within our pets vertical, we've been able to drive close to 1% order rate increases and 0.6% in active users.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, to conclude, there are three takeaways I would love for you to take away from this talk and how LLMs fit into search and recommendations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, discovery is a semantic understanding problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's not only about engagement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: LLMs give us a way to reason about item meaning and shopper intent, in DoorDash's case, for example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, distill LLM reasoning into primitives.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Capture reasoning offline as labels, semantic IDs, memory, and then let smaller and faster models serve it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The online LLM call is often not the product architecture you need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, shared representations create many use cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Once you have these primitives, they can power retrieval, ranking, content generation, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So last but not least, thank you, and thank you to all the collaborators at DoorDash.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have helped ship a lot of these things as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you.
